misconceptions.description: The learner treats any request for an average as a single procedure and does not separate averaging the function values from averaging its rate of change.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask which of the two answers carries the units of the function and which carries the units of a rate.
misconceptions.name: Average value and average rate of change are the same quantity

misconceptions.description: The learner sees the integral as the averaging operation itself, so the division by the length of the interval looks like an optional simplification.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask for the average value of the constant function two over an interval of length five.
misconceptions.name: The integral of a function is its average

misconceptions.description: The learner treats the integral expression as scratch work that supports the calculator rather than as the object being scored.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask the student to write, without the calculator, the expression whose value the calculator reported.
misconceptions.name: A calculator answer stands on its own

misconceptions.description: The learner treats the integral of velocity as the length of the trip, so the sign of the velocity plays no role.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Give a velocity that is positive on the first half of an interval and the negative of that on the second half, and ask for both quantities.
misconceptions.name: Distance travelled and net change in position are the same

misconceptions.description: The learner does not attach the absolute value to speed, so a negative speed is acceptable and the integrand for distance keeps its sign.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask for the speed of a particle whose velocity is a stated negative number.
misconceptions.name: Speed is another name for velocity

misconceptions.description: The learner reads an accumulation integral as the quantity itself rather than as the change in it, so the initial value has no role.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Give one rate and two different starting amounts and ask for the value at the later time in each case.
misconceptions.name: The integral of a rate is the amount of the quantity

misconceptions.description: The learner attaches accumulation to every rate in the problem without attending to the direction in which each one moves the quantity.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask what the stored amount does at a time when the two rates are equal.
misconceptions.name: Two rates acting at once combine by addition

misconceptions.description: The learner treats the first or second derivative test as a complete justification, so the endpoints of the interval are never considered.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Give a function whose only interior critical point is a relative maximum but whose largest value on the interval is at an endpoint.
misconceptions.name: A local extremum argument settles an absolute extremum

misconceptions.description: The learner treats the sentence as a label for the integral rather than as a statement that must fix the quantity, the interval, and the units.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask what would change in the sentence if the limits of the integral were different.
misconceptions.name: An interpretation is complete once the quantity is named

misconceptions.description: The learner treats area as always measured from the horizontal axis, so the second boundary curve is not subtracted.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask for the area between two horizontal lines and compare it with the integral of the upper line alone.
misconceptions.name: The area between curves is the integral of the curve that bounds it

misconceptions.description: The learner knows the area is positive and assumes any sign problem can be repaired at the end by taking the absolute value of the result.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask the student to write the statement that links the integral to the area and then to check it numerically.
misconceptions.name: The order of subtraction in an area integrand does not matter

misconceptions.description: The learner chooses limits from the axes of the picture or from the stated domain instead of from where the region actually begins and ends.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask which inputs bound the shaded region and why those and not the ends of the axes.
misconceptions.name: Limits of integration are a viewing window rather than a boundary

misconceptions.description: The learner treats dx and dy as labels for the direction of slicing rather than as the variable the integrand must be written in.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask the student to name every variable that appears in the integrand and compare it with the differential.
misconceptions.name: The differential can be changed without changing the integrand

misconceptions.description: The learner treats the area formula as a template applied once, so a crossing inside the interval does not signal that the region has pieces.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask for the sign of the integrand on each side of the interior crossing.
misconceptions.name: One integral covers any region between two curves

misconceptions.description: The learner associates pi with volume rather than with circular cross sections, so polygonal slices inherit it.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask which shape the area formula inside the integral describes.
misconceptions.name: Every volume integral carries a factor of pi

misconceptions.description: The learner reads the slice as reaching from the axis to the curve even when the region is bounded by two curves.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask the student to draw the slice on the figure and label both of its endpoints.
misconceptions.name: The cross sectional dimension is a function value

misconceptions.description: The learner treats squaring as distributing over subtraction, so a washer integrand is written with one squared difference.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask the student to evaluate both expressions with the radii five and three.
misconceptions.name: The difference of squares equals the square of the difference

misconceptions.description: The learner substitutes the distance between the boundary curves into every circular formula without asking whether it is a radius or a diameter.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask for the radius of a semicircle whose diameter is a stated length.
misconceptions.name: The distance between the curves is always the radius

misconceptions.description: The learner remembers the squared dimension but not the fraction in front of it, so equilateral, triangular, and semicircular sections lose their constants.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask for the area of one slice of the named shape with a numerical dimension.
misconceptions.name: Area formulas are recalled without their constant factors

misconceptions.description: The learner carries the circle formula only as far as the factor pi, so the radius is not squared inside the integral.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask for the area of a single disc of a stated radius before the integral is written.
misconceptions.name: A volume of revolution integrates the radius rather than its square

misconceptions.description: The learner treats the disc and washer formulas as fixed in the function rather than as built from a distance to the axis.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask for the distance from a named point on the curve to the stated axis of revolution.
misconceptions.name: The radius is the function value whatever the axis of revolution is

misconceptions.description: The learner treats the translation as applying to the whole integral rather than to the radius alone.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask which inputs the region occupies before the axis of revolution is named.
misconceptions.name: Moving the axis of revolution moves the limits of integration

misconceptions.description: The learner assigns the radii by position in the plane rather than by distance from the axis, which fails when the axis lies above the region.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Revolve the same region about a line above it and ask which curve is farther from that line.
misconceptions.name: The upper curve always gives the outer radius

misconceptions.description: The learner reads every definite integral as area under a graph, so a radical integrand is still described as an area and its own form is not examined.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask what integrand would give the area under the same graph and compare it with the one displayed.
misconceptions.name: An integral over an interval measures an area
